# All the funding deals in the femtech market

Last updated: 13 July 2026

Download **[our beautiful pitch about the femtech market](https://newmarketpitch.com/pages/femtech)**

![market research pitch 2026 statistics femtech market](https://cdn.shopify.com/s/files/1/0871/5413/1219/files/femtech-slides-chart.png?v=1771406109)

In **[our femtech market deck](https://newmarketpitch.com/pages/femtech)**, you will find everything you need to understand the market

The femtech market is attracting funding across fertility, maternity, menopause, diagnostics, pelvic health, and women’s clinical care.

We conducted deep research and collected 107 femtech market funding deals announced from 2024 through Q2 2026.

We refresh this femtech market funding page very often as companies announce new investment rounds.

And if you want to better understand this new industry, **[you should get our beautiful slides covering the femtech market](https://newmarketpitch.com/pages/femtech)**.

**Insights**

- The 107 femtech market funding deals represent about $1.84 billion in announced capital between 2024 and Q2 2026.
- Femtech market funding reached about $810 million in 2024, helped by large rounds for Flo Health, Maven Clinic, Comanche Biopharma, and Midi Health.
- Fertility remains one of the broadest femtech market segments, covering clinics, insurance, financing, diagnostics, embryo testing, laboratory automation, and reproductive biotechnology.
- Virtual women’s healthcare platforms are raising larger rounds as companies expand from one care area into broader services for women and families.
- Menopause care has become a major femtech market category, with repeated investments in Midi Health, Alloy, Coral, Elektra Health, Omena, and Evela Health.
- Several femtech companies raised more than once during the period, including Gameto, Gesynta Pharma, Midi Health, Pomelo Care, Samphire Neuroscience, Coral, and Ovum.
- Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in the femtech market for breast screening, prenatal imaging, fertility decisions, embryo assessment, and personalized maternal care.
- Medical devices remain important in femtech funding, especially for pelvic-floor conditions, urinary incontinence, childbirth, hormone monitoring, and breast pumping.
- The femtech market is becoming more global, with funded companies across North America, Europe, India, the Middle East, Japan, and Australia.

## Summary table of the funding deals for the femtech market since 2024

We define the femtech market as technology-enabled products and services that address women’s reproductive and other female-specific health needs.

We include solutions focused on menstrual and cycle health, fertility and contraception, pregnancy and postpartum, menopause, pelvic and sexual health, and clinically oriented tools for conditions that predominantly or uniquely affect women (e.g., breast and gynecological cancers).

We exclude general-purpose health, wellness, fitness, mental health, and consumer apps that are not specifically designed around women’s biology, care pathways, or life stages.

We focused exclusively on pure players, defined as companies with at least 70–80% of their business directly tied to the femtech market.

Our analysis has been done at a global level with a minimum funding threshold of $300k.

You can also read our detailed analysis to understand [how funding activity in the femtech market has evolved recently](https://newmarketpitch.com/blogs/news/femtech-funding-deals).

If you want a longer-term view, we also have [a study of how funding activity in the femtech market has changed over the years](https://newmarketpitch.com/blogs/news/femtech-funding-trends).

Also, you should know that we have a dedicated page, updated weekly, with [all the latest fundraising deals in the femtech market](https://newmarketpitch.com/blogs/news/femtech-funding-news).

I cross-checked company announcements, PR wires, investor/portfolio announcements, women’s-health funding trackers, and specialist healthtech media. Where the original round was disclosed in CAD, EUR, JPY, or AUD, I used the USD value stated in the source when available, or a rounded contemporaneous USD conversion when the source only gave local currency. ([The Origin Way][27]) I excluded non-dilutive grants from dollar totals where a source separated equity and grant funding; ScreenPoint is counted at $14M equity, not the full $16M headline amount. META-OBSERVATIONS 1. The 2026 YTD femtech funding market looks large because of scale rounds, not because the median company raised large amounts. The average round was $15.47M, but the median was only $7.00M, so any statement about “the typical femtech round” should use the median, not the average. 2. The top three deals captured 51.70% of all capital, which means YTD 2026 funding is best interpreted as a concentration story before it is interpreted as a broad market-growth story. A single omitted or reclassified large deal would materially change the market narrative. 3. Pregnancy Care Solutions led capital with 32.57% of dollars even though it represented only 21.43% of deals. That suggests investor conviction was strongest where products could connect to payer savings, birth-outcome data, hospital workflows, or clinical-risk reduction. 4. Hormonal Health Platforms had the highest non-singleton capital-share/deal-share ratio at 1.59, showing that menopause and hormone infrastructure moved from “underserved theme” into a category capable of attracting scaled growth checks. Midi’s $100M round explains much of this, but Clair and Osteoboost show the category is not only a one-company story. 5. Women’s Primary Care had the most deals but under-indexed heavily on capital, with 25.00% of deals but only 13.05% of dollars. The category is broad and active, but investors still appear to reserve the largest checks for clearer reimbursement, diagnostics, maternity-risk, or hormone-management pathways. 6. Fertility Care Platforms also under-indexed on capital share despite six deals. This implies that fertility remains formation-heavy in 2026 YTD, but the largest fertility-infrastructure checks seen in prior periods did not dominate this particular YTD window. 7. Seed rounds were 39.29% of deals but only 10.10% of capital, proving that founder formation is alive while scale capital remains selective. The market has many new experiments, but the money is still concentrated in companies with prior validation. 8. Series C and Series D+ together represented only 3 deals but 51.70% of all capital. This is a strong sign that late-stage femtech capital exists, but only for companies that have already passed strong evidence thresholds. 9. North America’s 80.27% capital share versus 64.29% deal share shows a funding-density advantage, not merely a company-count advantage. The region is where femtech companies are most likely to convert category validation into large checks. 10. Asia-Pacific generated 21.43% of deals but only 11.89% of capital, suggesting meaningful company creation without equivalent late-stage capital depth. The region appears active, but its rounds were mostly smaller except for Pee Safe. 11. Europe’s deal count was low but its median deal size was not weak because BrightHeart and ScreenPoint were clinically credible AI/diagnostics companies. The issue is not that European femtech rounds are necessarily tiny; it is that there were few disclosed qualifying rounds. 12. The absence of Latin America and Africa in the qualifying disclosed dataset should be read as a visibility and venture-financing gap, not an absence-of-need signal. The disease burden and access gaps are likely present, but they are not yet showing up in disclosed equity rounds above $300K under this definition. 13. Women’s oncology and diagnostics appeared repeatedly through Feminai, ScreenPoint, Mammogen, and Intu Diagnostics. This indicates that femtech funding is expanding beyond reproductive-life-stage apps into female-specific diagnostic infrastructure. 14. “AI” was common in the dataset, but AI alone did not explain funding strength. The better rule is that AI attracted capital when attached to a specific clinical workflow: prenatal ultrasound, fetal monitoring, oocyte assessment, breast screening, women’s primary care triage, or hormone monitoring. 15. The strongest rounds were attached to measurable economic or clinical bottlenecks: preterm birth, menopause care access, fertility cost, breast-cancer detection, postpartum hemorrhage, and hormonal monitoring. Investor appetite appears strongest when the company can plausibly connect female-specific biology to cost reduction, better diagnosis, or care-capacity expansion. 16. First financings were 25.00% of deals but only 7.54% of dollars, which means new-company formation is visible but not yet moving the capital totals. The market’s headline dollars are mostly a follow-on financing signal. 17. The bottom half of deals captured only 10.70% of capital, which shows the long tail is real but financially small. This matters for market sizing because counting companies produces a broader-looking market than counting dollars. 18. The 34-day gap between February 3 and March 10 shows that deal flow was not continuous even in an active market. Femtech in YTD 2026 should be described as lumpy and event-driven, not as a steady monthly funding wave. 19. Repeat-investor concentration was surprisingly low: only three investor names appeared in more than one qualifying deal. That suggests the sector is not yet dominated by a dense syndicate of repeat femtech specialists; rather, rounds are still being assembled from a fragmented mix of generalist, healthcare, regional, and strategic investors. 20. The dataset rewards companies that can leave the “consumer women’s wellness” frame. The largest checks clustered around virtual clinical care, regulated/cleared devices, diagnostics, maternity monitoring, and fertility infrastructure, while menstrual and broad primary-care platforms generated more deals but lower median dollars. metadata.twitter:description: All the fundraising deals made in the femtech market during Here is the full list of fundraising deals for Ytd 2026:FEMTECH MARKET — YTD 2026, JANUARY 1, 2026 THROUGH JULY 2, 2026 Research breakdown used to get to high confidence: I treated femtech as technology-enabled products and services addressing women’s reproductive and female-specific health needs: fertility, pregnancy/postpartum, menstrual health, hormonal/menopause care, pelvic health, women’s primary care, and breast or gynecological oncology/diagnostics. I cross-checked company announcements, PR wires, investor/portfolio announcements, women’s-health funding trackers, and specialist healthtech media. I excluded debt-only facilities, grants where equity was not disclosed, male contraception, generic wellness/fitness/obesity/mental-health platforms, non-pure-play digital health, and companies where the female-specific use case appeared incidental rather than more than 80% of the business. META-OBSERVATIONS 1. The 2026 YTD femtech funding market looks large because of scale rounds, not because the median company raised large amounts. The average round was $15.47M, but the median was only $7.00M, so any statement about “the typical femtech round” should use the median, not the average. 2. The top three deals captured 51.70% of all capital, which means YTD 2026 funding is best interpreted as a concentration story before it is interpreted as a broad market-growth story. A single omitted or reclassified large deal would materially change the market narrative. 3. Pregnancy Care Solutions led capital with 32.57% of dollars even though it represented only 21.43% of deals. That suggests investor conviction was strongest where products could connect to payer savings, birth-outcome data, hospital workflows, or clinical-risk reduction. 4. Hormonal Health Platforms had the highest non-singleton capital-share/deal-share ratio at 1.59, showing that menopause and hormone infrastructure moved from “underserved theme” into a category capable of attracting scaled growth checks. Midi’s $100M round explains much of this, but Clair and Osteoboost show the category is not only a one-company story. 5. Women’s Primary Care had the most deals but under-indexed heavily on capital, with 25.00% of deals but only 13.05% of dollars. The category is broad and active, but investors still appear to reserve the largest checks for clearer reimbursement, diagnostics, maternity-risk, or hormone-management pathways. 6. Fertility Care Platforms also under-indexed on capital share despite six deals. This implies that fertility remains formation-heavy in 2026 YTD, but the largest fertility-infrastructure checks seen in prior periods did not dominate this particular YTD window. 7. Seed rounds were 39.29% of deals but only 10.10% of capital, proving that founder formation is alive while scale capital remains selective. The market has many new experiments, but the money is still concentrated in companies with prior validation. 8. Series C and Series D+ together represented only 3 deals but 51.70% of all capital. This is a strong sign that late-stage femtech capital exists, but only for companies that have already passed strong evidence thresholds. 9. North America’s 80.27% capital share versus 64.29% deal share shows a funding-density advantage, not merely a company-count advantage. The region is where femtech companies are most likely to convert category validation into large checks. 10. Asia-Pacific generated 21.43% of deals but only 11.89% of capital, suggesting meaningful company creation without equivalent late-stage capital depth. The region appears active, but its rounds were mostly smaller except for Pee Safe. 11. Europe’s deal count was low but its median deal size was not weak because BrightHeart and ScreenPoint were clinically credible AI/diagnostics companies. The issue is not that European femtech rounds are necessarily tiny; it is that there were few disclosed qualifying rounds. 12. The absence of Latin America and Africa in the qualifying disclosed dataset should be read as a visibility and venture-financing gap, not an absence-of-need signal. The disease burden and access gaps are likely present, but they are not yet showing up in disclosed equity rounds above $300K under this definition. 13. Women’s oncology and diagnostics appeared repeatedly through Feminai, ScreenPoint, Mammogen, and Intu Diagnostics. This indicates that femtech funding is expanding beyond reproductive-life-stage apps into female-specific diagnostic infrastructure. 14. “AI” was common in the dataset, but AI alone did not explain funding strength. The better rule is that AI attracted capital when attached to a specific clinical workflow: prenatal ultrasound, fetal monitoring, oocyte assessment, breast screening, women’s primary care triage, or hormone monitoring. 15. The strongest rounds were attached to measurable economic or clinical bottlenecks: preterm birth, menopause care access, fertility cost, breast-cancer detection, postpartum hemorrhage, and hormonal monitoring. Investor appetite appears strongest when the company can plausibly connect female-specific biology to cost reduction, better diagnosis, or care-capacity expansion. 16. First financings were 25.00% of deals but only 7.54% of dollars, which means new-company formation is visible but not yet moving the capital totals. The market’s headline dollars are mostly a follow-on financing signal. 17. The bottom half of deals captured only 10.70% of capital, which shows the long tail is real but financially small. This matters for market sizing because counting companies produces a broader-looking market than counting dollars. 18. The 34-day gap between February 3 and March 10 shows that deal flow was not continuous even in an active market. Femtech in YTD 2026 should be described as lumpy and event-driven, not as a steady monthly funding wave. 19. Repeat-investor concentration was surprisingly low: only three investor names appeared in more than one qualifying deal. That suggests the sector is not yet dominated by a dense syndicate of repeat femtech specialists; rather, rounds are still being assembled from a fragmented mix of generalist, healthcare, regional, and strategic investors. 20. The dataset rewards companies that can leave the “consumer women’s wellness” frame. The largest checks clustered around virtual clinical care, regulated/cleared devices, diagnostics, maternity monitoring, and fertility infrastructure, while menstrual and broad primary-care platforms generated more deals but lower median dollars. META-OBSERVATIONS 1. The 2026 YTD femtech funding market looks large because of scale rounds, not because the median company raised large amounts. The average round was $15.47M, but the median was only $7.00M, so any statement about “the typical femtech round” should use the median, not the average. 2. The top three deals captured 51.70% of all capital, which means YTD 2026 funding is best interpreted as a concentration story before it is interpreted as a broad market-growth story. A single omitted or reclassified large deal would materially change the market narrative. 3. Pregnancy Care Solutions led capital with 32.57% of dollars even though it represented only 21.43% of deals. That suggests investor conviction was strongest where products could connect to payer savings, birth-outcome data, hospital workflows, or clinical-risk reduction. 4. Hormonal Health Platforms had the highest non-singleton capital-share/deal-share ratio at 1.59, showing that menopause and hormone infrastructure moved from “underserved theme” into a category capable of attracting scaled growth checks. Midi’s $100M round explains much of this, but Clair and Osteoboost show the category is not only a one-company story. 5. Women’s Primary Care had the most deals but under-indexed heavily on capital, with 25.00% of deals but only 13.05% of dollars. The category is broad and active, but investors still appear to reserve the largest checks for clearer reimbursement, diagnostics, maternity-risk, or hormone-management pathways. 6. Fertility Care Platforms also under-indexed on capital share despite six deals. This implies that fertility remains formation-heavy in 2026 YTD, but the largest fertility-infrastructure checks seen in prior periods did not dominate this particular YTD window. 7. Seed rounds were 39.29% of deals but only 10.10% of capital, proving that founder formation is alive while scale capital remains selective. The market has many new experiments, but the money is still concentrated in companies with prior validation. 8. Series C and Series D+ together represented only 3 deals but 51.70% of all capital. This is a strong sign that late-stage femtech capital exists, but only for companies that have already passed strong evidence thresholds. 9. North America’s 80.27% capital share versus 64.29% deal share shows a funding-density advantage, not merely a company-count advantage. The region is where femtech companies are most likely to convert category validation into large checks. 10. Asia-Pacific generated 21.43% of deals but only 11.89% of capital, suggesting meaningful company creation without equivalent late-stage capital depth. The region appears active, but its rounds were mostly smaller except for Pee Safe. 11. Europe’s deal count was low but its median deal size was not weak because BrightHeart and ScreenPoint were clinically credible AI/diagnostics companies. The issue is not that European femtech rounds are necessarily tiny; it is that there were few disclosed qualifying rounds. 12. The absence of Latin America and Africa in the qualifying disclosed dataset should be read as a visibility and venture-financing gap, not an absence-of-need signal. The disease burden and access gaps are likely present, but they are not yet showing up in disclosed equity rounds above $300K under this definition. 13. Women’s oncology and diagnostics appeared repeatedly through Feminai, ScreenPoint, Mammogen, and Intu Diagnostics. This indicates that femtech funding is expanding beyond reproductive-life-stage apps into female-specific diagnostic infrastructure. 14. “AI” was common in the dataset, but AI alone did not explain funding strength. The better rule is that AI attracted capital when attached to a specific clinical workflow: prenatal ultrasound, fetal monitoring, oocyte assessment, breast screening, women’s primary care triage, or hormone monitoring. 15. The strongest rounds were attached to measurable economic or clinical bottlenecks: preterm birth, menopause care access, fertility cost, breast-cancer detection, postpartum hemorrhage, and hormonal monitoring. Investor appetite appears strongest when the company can plausibly connect female-specific biology to cost reduction, better diagnosis, or care-capacity expansion. 16. First financings were 25.00% of deals but only 7.54% of dollars, which means new-company formation is visible but not yet moving the capital totals. The market’s headline dollars are mostly a follow-on financing signal. 17. The bottom half of deals captured only 10.70% of capital, which shows the long tail is real but financially small. This matters for market sizing because counting companies produces a broader-looking market than counting dollars. 18. The 34-day gap between February 3 and March 10 shows that deal flow was not continuous even in an active market. Femtech in YTD 2026 should be described as lumpy and event-driven, not as a steady monthly funding wave. 19. Repeat-investor concentration was surprisingly low: only three investor names appeared in more than one qualifying deal. That suggests the sector is not yet dominated by a dense syndicate of repeat femtech specialists; rather, rounds are still being assembled from a fragmented mix of generalist, healthcare, regional, and strategic investors. 20. META-OBSERVATIONS 1. The 2026 YTD femtech funding market looks large because of scale rounds, not because the median company raised large amounts. The average round was $15.47M, but the median was only $7.00M, so any statement about “the typical femtech round” should use the median, not the average. 2. The top three deals captured 51.70% of all capital, which means YTD 2026 funding is best interpreted as a concentration story before it is interpreted as a broad market-growth story. A single omitted or reclassified large deal would materially change the market narrative. 3. Pregnancy Care Solutions led capital with 32.57% of dollars even though it represented only 21.43% of deals. That suggests investor conviction was strongest where products could connect to payer savings, birth-outcome data, hospital workflows, or clinical-risk reduction. 4. Hormonal Health Platforms had the highest non-singleton capital-share/deal-share ratio at 1.59, showing that menopause and hormone infrastructure moved from “underserved theme” into a category capable of attracting scaled growth checks. Midi’s $100M round explains much of this, but Clair and Osteoboost show the category is not only a one-company story. 5. Women’s Primary Care had the most deals but under-indexed heavily on capital, with 25.00% of deals but only 13.05% of dollars. The category is broad and active, but investors still appear to reserve the largest checks for clearer reimbursement, diagnostics, maternity-risk, or hormone-management pathways. 6. Fertility Care Platforms also under-indexed on capital share despite six deals. This implies that fertility remains formation-heavy in 2026 YTD, but the largest fertility-infrastructure checks seen in prior periods did not dominate this particular YTD window. 7. Seed rounds were 39.29% of deals but only 10.10% of capital, proving that founder formation is alive while scale capital remains selective. The market has many new experiments, but the money is still concentrated in companies with prior validation. 8. Series C and Series D+ together represented only 3 deals but 51.70% of all capital. This is a strong sign that late-stage femtech capital exists, but only for companies that have already passed strong evidence thresholds. 9. North America’s 80.27% capital share versus 64.29% deal share shows a funding-density advantage, not merely a company-count advantage. The region is where femtech companies are most likely to convert category validation into large checks. 10. Asia-Pacific generated 21.43% of deals but only 11.89% of capital, suggesting meaningful company creation without equivalent late-stage capital depth. The region appears active, but its rounds were mostly smaller except for Pee Safe. 11. Europe’s deal count was low but its median deal size was not weak because BrightHeart and ScreenPoint were clinically credible AI/diagnostics companies. The issue is not that European femtech rounds are necessarily tiny; it is that there were few disclosed qualifying rounds. 12. The absence of Latin America and Africa in the qualifying disclosed dataset should be read as a visibility and venture-financing gap, not an absence-of-need signal. The disease burden and access gaps are likely present, but they are not yet showing up in disclosed equity rounds above $300K under this definition. 13. Women’s oncology and diagnostics appeared repeatedly through Feminai, ScreenPoint, Mammogen, and Intu Diagnostics. This indicates that femtech funding is expanding beyond reproductive-life-stage apps into female-specific diagnostic infrastructure. 14. “AI” was common in the dataset, but AI alone did not explain funding strength. The better rule is that AI attracted capital when attached to a specific clinical workflow: prenatal ultrasound, fetal monitoring, oocyte assessment, breast screening, women’s primary care triage, or hormone monitoring. 15. The strongest rounds were attached to measurable economic or clinical bottlenecks: preterm birth, menopause care access, fertility cost, breast-cancer detection, postpartum hemorrhage, and hormonal monitoring. Investor appetite appears strongest when the company can plausibly connect female-specific biology to cost reduction, better diagnosis, or care-capacity expansion. 16. First financings were 25.00% of deals but only 7.54% of dollars, which means new-company formation is visible but not yet moving the capital totals. The market’s headline dollars are mostly a follow-on financing signal. 17. The bottom half of deals captured only 10.70% of capital, which shows the long tail is real but financially small. This matters for market sizing because counting companies produces a broader-looking market than counting dollars. 18. The 34-day gap between February 3 and March 10 shows that deal flow was not continuous even in an active market. Femtech in YTD 2026 should be described as lumpy and event-driven, not as a steady monthly funding wave. 19. Repeat-investor concentration was surprisingly low: only three investor names appeared in more than one qualifying deal. That suggests the sector is not yet dominated by a dense syndicate of repeat femtech specialists; rather, rounds are still being assembled from a fragmented mix of generalist, healthcare, regional, and strategic investors. 20. The dataset rewards companies that can leave the “consumer women’s wellness” frame. The largest checks clustered around virtual clinical care, regulated/cleared devices, diagnostics, maternity monitoring, and fertility infrastructure, while menstrual and broad primary-care platforms generated more deals but lower median dollars.
